message.content:
Below are three practical ways to capture a screenshot of a web page that is (or will be) displayed in Google Chrome, all from a Python script. | Method | When to use it | What you need | Quick code snippet | |--------|----------------|---------------|--------------------| | **Selenium WebDriver** | You want to *control* Chrome (open a URL, click buttons, etc.) and then take a screenshot. | `selenium` package + ChromeDriver (or `webdriver-manager` to auto‑download it). | ```python
from selenium import webdriver
from selenium.webdriver.chrome.service import Service
from webdriver_manager.chrome import ChromeDriverManager

options = webdriver.ChromeOptions()
options.add_argument("--headless") # optional – run without opening a window
driver = webdriver.Chrome(service=Service(ChromeDriverManager().install()), options=options)
driver.get("https://www.example.com")
driver.save_screenshot("example.png")
driver.quit()
``` | | **Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP)** | You already have Chrome running (or you want to attach to an existing instance) and you don’t want to launch a new browser process. | `pychrome` (or `chrome-devtools-protocol`), Chrome must be started with `--remote-debugging-port=9222`. | ```python
import pychrome

browser = pychrome.Browser(url="http://127.0.0.1:9222")
tab = browser.list_tab()[0] # first tab
tab.start()
tab.call_method("Page.navigate", url="https://www.example.com")
tab.wait(5) # wait for page load
result = tab.call_method("Page.captureScreenshot")
with open("example.png", "wb") as f:
f.write(bytes.fromhex(result["data"]))
tab.stop()
``` | | **PyAutoGUI / Pillow** | You just want a *pixel‑perfect* screenshot of whatever is currently visible on your screen (including Chrome’s UI). | `pyautogui` (and optionally `pillow`). | ```python
import pyautogui
image = pyautogui.screenshot() # full screen
image.save("full_screen.png")
``` | --- ## 1. Selenium WebDriver – the most common approach ### Install the dependencies ```bash pip install selenium webdriver-manager ``` > **Tip:** `webdriver-manager` automatically downloads the correct ChromeDriver binary for your Chrome version, so you don’t have to manage it manually. ### Full example ```python import time from selenium import webdriver from selenium.webdriver.chrome.service import Service from webdriver_manager.chrome import ChromeDriverManager def screenshot_url(url: str, out_path: str, headless: bool = True): options = webdriver.ChromeOptions() if headless: options.add_argument("--headless") # no GUI options.add_argument("--disable-gpu") # needed on Windows options.add_argument("--window-size=1920,1080") # set viewport size # Create the driver driver = webdriver.Chrome( service=Service(ChromeDriverManager().install()), options=options ) try: driver.get(url) # Optional: wait for dynamic content to load time.sleep(2) # or use WebDriverWait for a specific element driver.save_screenshot(out_path) print(f"Screenshot saved to {out_path}") finally: driver.quit() if __name__ == "__main__": screenshot_url("https://www.python.org", "python_home.png") ``` **What it does** 1. Starts Chrome (headless or normal). 2. Navigates to the URL. 3. Waits a bit for the page to finish rendering. 4. Calls `save_screenshot`, which writes a PNG file. --- ## 2. Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP) If you already have Chrome running and you want to attach to it, start Chrome with a debugging port: ```bash chrome.exe --remote-debugging-port=9222 ``` Then use `pychrome`: ```bash pip install pychrome ``` ```python import pychrome def screenshot_cdp(url: str, out_path: str): browser = pychrome.Browser(url="http://127.0.0.1:9222") tab = browser.list_tab()[0] # pick the first tab tab.start() tab.call_method("Page.navigate", url=url) tab.wait(5) # wait for load result = tab.call_method("Page.captureScreenshot") with open(out_path, "wb") as f: f.write(bytes.fromhex(result["data"])) tab.stop() if __name__ == "__main__": screenshot_cdp("https://www.wikipedia.org", "wiki.png") ``` **Why use CDP?** - No need to launch a new Chrome process. - Works even if you’re already interacting with Chrome manually. - Gives you low‑level control (e.g., capture a specific element). --- ## 3. PyAutoGUI – screenshot of the *visible* screen If you simply want a screenshot of whatever is on your monitor (including the Chrome window, toolbar, etc.), `pyautogui` is the quickest way: ```bash pip install pyautogui pillow ``` ```python import pyautogui # Full screen pyautogui.screenshot("full_screen.png") # Or a region: (left, top, width, height) region = (100, 200, 800, 600) pyautogui.screenshot("region.png", region=region) ``` > **Note:** This captures the *pixel* contents of the screen, not the DOM. It’s useful for UI testing or when you need an exact visual snapshot. --- ## Choosing the right method | Scenario | Recommended method | |----------|--------------------| | Automate navigation, click, fill forms, then screenshot | Selenium | | Attach to an already‑running Chrome instance | CDP (`pychrome`) | | Capture the exact pixels on your monitor | PyAutoGUI | --- ## Common pitfalls & troubleshooting | Problem | Fix | |---------|-----| | **ChromeDriver version mismatch** | Use `webdriver-manager` or download the matching driver from . | | **Headless screenshots look blurry** | Set a larger viewport: `options.add_argument("--window-size=1920,1080")`. | | **Page not fully loaded before screenshot** | Use `WebDriverWait` instead of `time.sleep`. Example: `WebDriverWait(driver, 10).until(EC.presence_of_element_located((By.TAG_NAME, "body")))`. | | **CDP fails to connect** | Ensure Chrome was started with `--remote-debugging-port=9222` and that no firewall blocks the port. | | **PyAutoGUI fails on macOS** | Install `pillow` and `pyobjc-framework-Quartz` (`pip install pyobjc`). | --- ## Wrap‑up With any of the three approaches above you can capture a screenshot of a web page shown in Google Chrome using Python. Pick the one that best fits your workflow: - **Selenium** for full automation. - **CDP** for attaching to an existing Chrome session. - **PyAutoGUI** for a quick pixel‑perfect screen grab. Happy coding!
